retro.headline: Assessors will recommend a single (not split) tax rate and rejecting all three optional exemptions for FY2026
retro.summary: The Board of Assessors reviewed FY2026 valuation and growth figures, worked through mapping and MUNIS data delays, and discussed hiring a third party to redo property neighborhoods after a citizen work group flagged inconsistent boundaries. Most of the meeting was spent line-editing a classification-hearing presentation, ending in board recommendations to reject the residential, open-space, and small commercial exemptions and to keep a single tax rate, plus review of a fall town meeting exemption/COLA warrant article and website fixes.

what_happened.line: The Board of Assessors recommended a single, not split, tax rate for FY2026.
The board voted to reject adopting the residential exemption for the FY2026 classification.
The board also voted to reject adopting the small commercial exemption for FY2026.
The board leaned toward hiring an outside firm, rather than the citizen work group, to redo property-neighborhood boundaries after inconsistencies were flagged.
The assessor said the printed fall town meeting warrant article understated the cost of adopting COLA-linked exemption updates as zero and said it needs correcting before town meeting.

why_it_matters: A single versus split tax rate changes how the tax levy is divided between residential and commercial/industrial property, which shows up directly in individual tax bills.
Declining the residential and small commercial exemptions means the classification hearing will not shift additional tax burden between property types beyond the rate decision itself.

The COLA-linked exemption warrant article, once its cost is corrected, goes to voters at fall town meeting and is paid from the overlay account, meaning any expansion is funded by other taxpayers rather than the town budget.
watch_next: November 20 Board of Assessors meeting, including a planned resident outreach conference on abatements and exemptions
The fall town meeting warrant article on COLA adjustments to Clauses 41C/41D/17D/17E/17F, once its cost figure is corrected

retro.headline: APDC sent legal questions on its demolition bylaw to executive session amid a push to merge with the Historical Commission
retro.summary: The Architectural Preservation District Commission welcomed the town's new land use director, approved prior minutes, and spent most of the meeting on a proposed merger with the Historical Commission, moving unresolved legal questions about the APD bylaw's enforceability to executive session. Members also discussed the troubled Ritter/Town Hall renovation design process, agreed to digitize the determination-of-applicability form via OpenGov.com, and reviewed building-repair, Brooks house, and cemetery-restoration project updates.

what_happened.line: The commission sent open legal questions about the demolition bylaw's enforceability into executive session amid a push to merge with the Historical Commission.
Members leaned toward merging the two boards into one, while keeping the historic district's current boundaries, pending legal review.
A member was tasked with drafting bylaw and design-guideline changes for the merger to bring back in February, after the chair pulls the bylaw's Attorney General review file.
The commission agreed to move its determination-of-applicability form onto the town's OpenGov.com system.
The next meeting was set for February 13.

why_it_matters: A merger would change which board reviews demolition and renovation requests inside the Architectural Preservation District, and the bylaw's enforceability is itself in question.
watch_next: February 13 meeting, when drafted bylaw and design-guideline changes for the merger return
the Attorney General review file on the APD bylaw

retro.headline: FinCom will likely fund an outside review of the school department's FY26 budget overruns from its reserve
retro.summary: The Finance Committee got a preliminary, informational run-through of draft special town meeting warrant articles (zoning, stormwater fees, a veterans' exemption increase, PAC salaries, a $195,830 track/turf engineering request, and a special education reserve fund transfer) ahead of an October 8 discussion and October 22 public hearing for a November 17 special town meeting. The bulk of the meeting concerned a planned outside financial operations review of the school department's FY26 budget variance, to be funded from the Finance Committee's reserve account once a firm and scope are chosen; members also discussed possible tri-board meetings, a DLS workshop on financial policy, and committee reports on the municipal building project, the library, and the school finance director search.

what_happened.line: The Finance Committee expects to fund an outside review of the school department's FY26 budget variance from its own reserve account.

Draft special town meeting articles got a first look -- stormwater fees, a veterans' exemption increase, PAC salaries, a track/turf field engineering request, and a special education reserve transfer.
Those articles move to an in-depth discussion October 8 and a public hearing October 22, ahead of a November 17 special town meeting.
A workshop on net school spending was tabled because the presenter could not attend.
Whether to hold joint tri-board meetings, on topics including an athletics budget and ambulance billing write-offs, was left to the three board chairs to work out.

why_it_matters: The planned review would look at why the school department's FY26 spending diverged from its budget, a question tied to special education placement costs.
The special education reserve transfer, the track/turf field funding, and a possible veterans' exemption increase would all go to voters at the November 17 special town meeting.
A new stormwater fee structure, discussed at this meeting, could show up as a separate charge on future bills depending on how the article is written.
watch_next: October 8 in-depth discussion of the special town meeting warrant articles
November 17 special town meeting

retro.headline: Paraprofessional contract vote delayed again over salary-calculation errors; two placeholder warrant articles advanced
retro.summary: The School Committee heard that the top business-administrator candidate withdrew and that a UMass Boston review of district financial practices is being scoped, and it postponed ratifying the paraprofessional contract again after discovering salary-scale calculation errors. Members voted to place placeholder warrant articles on the November town meeting warrant for a special education stabilization fund and for a turf field/track feasibility study, approved an eighth-grade Washington DC trip switching to train travel, changed the LHS spring parent-teacher conference date, adopted operating protocols, and reviewed the superintendent's draft evaluation goals and school committee goals, including ongoing finance-office staffing concerns.

what_happened.line: The committee again passed over ratifying the paraprofessional contract after salary-scale calculation errors were found.
Members voted unanimously to send a placeholder warrant article for a special education stabilization fund toward November town meeting.
A placeholder warrant article seeking money for a feasibility and schematic study of the turf field, track, drainage and retaining wall passed 5-0.
The committee passed over the business administrator position after its top candidate withdrew, and the job was reposted with a revised description and a higher salary range.
Members approved the eighth-grade Washington DC trip, switching student travel from a prior mode to train.

why_it_matters: A further delay in ratifying the paraprofessional contract means paraprofessionals' pay under the new agreement remains unsettled.
The two placeholder warrant articles put a special education stabilization fund and a turf field/track study before voters at the November town meeting.
The unfilled business administrator post, alongside a financial practices review with UMass Boston, touches who oversees the school budget while that review is underway.
watch_next: November town meeting warrant: votes on the special education stabilization fund and the turf field/track feasibility study articles
A future School Committee vote on reratifying the corrected paraprofessional contract

retro.headline: Conservation Commission approved the Lake Shirley boat ramp rebuild with wetland buffer waivers.
retro.summary: The Lunenburg Conservation Commission held a long session covering multiple RDAs, NOIs, tree-removal determinations and a certificate of compliance, approving several routine wetland-adjacent projects (a cemetery expansion, septic repairs, a shed/sand permit, tree removals) with standard conditions. The major substantive action was approval of the Shady Point boat ramp reconstruction on Lake Shirley with buffer-zone waivers after public debate over impervious-surface classification and a retaining wall versus riprap; several other hearings (404 Page Street, 108 Sunny Hill Road, the Violet irrigation pond, 141 Pleasant Street) were continued to October 7. The commission also discussed Hollis Road residence budget items, a storm water utility warrant article, and a resolved no-trespass situation at the Pleasant Street Conservation Area.

what_happened.line: The commission approved the Lake Shirley boat ramp rebuild at Shady Point, granting waivers to work inside the normal 30-foot no-disturb and 50-foot no-build wetland buffers.
Four other wetland hearings, including a new house and driveway at 404 Page Street, were continued to October 7 rather than decided.
The commission approved three routine RDAs with standard conditions: a DPW cemetery expansion, a septic force main repair, and a shed/sand permit.
A non-binding warrant article was finalized asking whether storm water funding should move out of the operating budget into a dedicated storm water utility.
A vote on replacing flooring at the town-owned Hollis Road residence was deferred pending clarification of a vendor's deposit request.

why_it_matters: The boat ramp decision sets a precedent for allowing construction inside protected wetland buffers along Lake Shirley when a project shows a public benefit.

The storm water warrant article, if it reaches town meeting, would ask voters to decide whether storm water work gets its own dedicated funding stream instead of competing inside the general operating budget.
Residents near 404 Page Street, 108 Sunny Hill Road, the Violet irrigation pond, and 141 Pleasant Street will have another chance to be heard before any of those projects are decided.
watch_next: October 7, 2026: continued hearings for 404 Page Street, 108 Sunny Hill Road, the Violet irrigation pond, and 141 Pleasant Street
The storm water utility warrant article, as submitted for an upcoming town meeting

retro.headline: Select Board advanced the Food Pantry's temporary move to 30 School Street, waiving fees and OK'ing a license.
retro.summary: The board presented three staff Merit Awards, publicly introduced new town manager Jessica "Jack" Miller, and voted to authorize a license agreement and waive building fees advancing the Lunenburg Food Pantry's temporary relocation to 30 School Street, amid public-comment dispute over whether that structure is "permanent" or "temporary." The board also referred zoning cleanup and stormwater-fee articles to the planning board for the November special town meeting, accepted a donated boulder for town hall, discussed but declined for now a MassWorks grant to study senior housing at the former TCP school, and debated (and largely declined) moving to a biweekly meeting schedule.

what_happened.line: Select Board authorized a license agreement and waived building-department fees to advance the Food Pantry's move to 30 School Street.
A resident disputed the building commissioner's call that the new structure counts as permanent rather than temporary.
Board publicly introduced incoming town manager Jessica "Jack" Miller.
Zoning cleanup and a stormwater fee-bylaw article were referred to the planning board for the November 17 special town meeting.
Board declined to pursue a MassWorks grant this cycle to study senior housing at the former TCP school, citing a need for more public discussion.

why_it_matters: The food pantry's site status and its permanent-vs-temporary classification affect what oversight and process apply to future town-building decisions.
The stormwater bylaw change would tie fee amounts to a planning-board schedule that can change without a town meeting vote, which residents will be asked to weigh in November.
Passing on the MassWorks grant this cycle means no funded study of TCP senior housing for now, leaving that option undecided.
watch_next: November 17 special town meeting: zoning and stormwater fee articles, plus the Brooks House sale/lease report
FY26 budget close-out figures, expected in roughly two to three weeks

retro.headline: Open Space Committee reelected its chair and began rewriting land-acquisition criteria, to return in October
retro.summary: The Lunenburg Open Space Committee held its first meeting since June, approved the May minutes, and re-elected its officers (Mike Hill as chair, Anna as vice chair, Eric as clerk) under a new term-limit bylaw. Most of the meeting was spent workshopping proposed revisions to the open space acquisition criteria -- parcel size tiers, habitat resources, public access, scenic vistas, contiguous parcels, and agricultural viability -- with the chair agreeing to rework the wording based on member feedback and bring it back in October.

what_happened.line: The committee re-elected Mike Hill as chair, Anna as vice chair, and Eric as clerk, each by unanimous roll call under a newly adopted term-limit bylaw.

Members spent most of the meeting workshopping revisions to the criteria used to prioritize land for open space acquisition, including parcel size, habitat, public access, scenic vistas, contiguous parcels, and farmland viability.
No vote was taken on the criteria; the chair agreed to rework the wording based on member feedback and bring a revised draft back in October.

The chair will check with the conservation commission, planning board, and parks department on whether their appointed representatives to this committee will continue, since the new bylaw sets term limits and a reappointment process.

why_it_matters: The criteria under revision are what the town uses to decide which parcels get prioritized for conservation purchase or protection, so the wording adopted in October will shape future land decisions.
The new term-limit bylaw affects who can serve on the committee and how other boards appoint their representatives to it.

retro.headline: Board withholds releasing a tax lien on a Chapter Land property until the owner pays years of back taxes owed.
retro.summary: The Board of Assessors reviewed routine business — prior minutes, excise tax abatement procedure, pending vision/commercial valuations, and new-growth estimates — then spent most of the meeting on a long-running dispute over a Chapter Land (CL9) property where the owner underpaid taxes for years; the board decided to keep the lien in place until back taxes are paid. It also discussed GIS/mapping software costs, an update to the veterans' property tax exemption for the November special town meeting, a staffing departure, and senior means-tested exemption applications, before adjourning into executive session.

what_happened.line: The board will not release the lien on a Chapter Land property until the town actually receives the owner's back-tax payment.
The town will not pursue rollback taxes on that property, instead collecting only the back taxes now owed on what has become three or four separate parcels.
The board agreed to seek a placeholder warrant article raising the veterans' property tax exemption for the November 17th special town meeting.
Review of August's already-processed excise tax abatements was pushed to the next meeting rather than taken up tonight.
The board reset its fall meeting schedule to September 23rd, October 14th, and October 28th.

why_it_matters: A property tax lien stays in force as leverage until back taxes are paid, and the town is not pursuing the larger rollback-tax penalty it could have sought on this Chapter Land property.
A veterans' exemption increase would go before voters as a warrant article at the November 17th special town meeting, and any increase is funded entirely by the town with no state reimbursement.
Routine items -- excise abatements, new-growth estimates, senior exemption applications -- remain in process rather than finalized this meeting.
watch_next: September 23rd Board of Assessors meeting -- veterans' exemption research
November 17th special town meeting -- veterans' exemption warrant article

retro.headline: DEP says every well must meet PFAS limits alone by 2029; blending won't count, forcing plant-vs-buy choice
retro.summary: The Water Commissioners reviewed warrants and minutes, then spent most of the meeting on MassDEP's PFAS ("PFOA/PFOS") requirements, learning that each individual well must independently meet the state limit by 2029 and that blending water from multiple sources will not be accepted as a permanent compliance strategy. The board discussed two paths forward -- building a treatment plant or purchasing water from Townsend -- without deciding between them, and separately took up bacteria failures at several wells, a proposal to fund cleaning of the Keings and Lancaster wells at a future special meeting, and connection-fee questions for the food pantry and a package store project.

what_happened.line: MassDEP told the district every well must meet PFAS limits on its own by 2029, and blending from multiple sources will not count as compliance, forcing a choice between a treatment plant or buying water elsewhere.
The board agreed to ask the town of Townsend in writing for a price to supply the district's water demand as an alternative to building a treatment plant, without choosing between the two paths.
Several wells are currently failing bacteria tests, prompting emergency chlorine dosing at one well.
The superintendent will gather quotes to clean the Keings and Lancaster wells and bring them to a future special meeting for the board to consider funding.
The board waived a new connection fee for the food pantry's relocation, citing a pre-existing connection, and set a conditional waiver for a package store project.

why_it_matters: Whichever path the district picks for PFAS compliance -- a treatment plant or buying water from Townsend -- is likely to show up on residents' water rates, and the board has not yet chosen or costed either option.
Bacteria failures at multiple wells and the emergency chlorine dosing concern the safety of water currently reaching customers' taps.
How the district treats connection fees on existing hookups, as decided here for the food pantry and a package store, sets a precedent other applicants may point to.
watch_next: Townsend's written price quote for supplying the district's water demand
A special meeting, expected in a low-usage period such as winter, to appropriate funds for cleaning the Keings and Lancaster wells

retro.headline: Town meeting approved the school department's full state-aid request over a select-board bid to cut it
retro.summary: This special town meeting was called by citizen petition mainly to decide how to allocate unanticipated state education aid and to restore cut middle-school sports. After an extended dispute over which vote threshold applies to different kinds of money articles and a lengthy sound-system delay, the meeting rejected a select-board amendment to reduce the school department's requested state-aid appropriation and approved the full amount for staffing, literacy and athletics needs. A second article was passed over, and a smaller transfer from a winter-recovery special revenue fund to restore middle-school sports and transportation was separately approved after the school committee and select board both endorsed it.

what_happened.line: Town meeting voted down a select-board amendment to cut the school department's requested state-aid appropriation, then approved the full amount.
The approved funds are earmarked for school staffing, K-12 literacy programming, and high school athletics transportation.

retro.headline: Personnel Committee unanimously approved the data collector job description as written, unchanged from its 2024 grade.
retro.summary: The three-member Personnel Committee met briefly by Zoom to review the Assessor's office data collector job description, last written in 2024. After discussing comparable-town pay data and whether the role's added valuation-and-appraisal duties warranted moving it from grade eight to grade nine, the committee voted unanimously to approve the description as written so the position could be posted immediately, leaving reclassification as a possible future revisit.

what_happened.line: The Personnel Committee voted unanimously to approve the Assessor's office data collector job description as written, without moving it up a pay grade.
The committee chose to post the position at its current grade rather than pursue reclassification first, so the hiring process would not be delayed.
The chair raised the idea of a bylaw requiring job descriptions to be reviewed periodically, so a case like this would not need to return to the committee; no vote was taken on it.
The next meeting will take up a newly submitted job description as a main agenda item.

why_it_matters: The decision lets the town post and fill the data collector opening at the Assessor's office immediately, rather than waiting on a pay-grade review.

Whether the role should move to a higher grade -- raised because of added valuation-and-appraisal duties and comparable-town pay data -- was left open rather than resolved, and could resurface as a cost to a future budget.
A possible bylaw change to require regular review of town job descriptions was floated but not voted on, and would affect how future personnel decisions like this one get made.

retro.headline: Commission voted to redesign the Cowry Nature Center ADA trail route to avoid direct wetland alteration.
retro.summary: The Conservation Commission heard an extended public comment from a former commissioner about hearing-process fairness, then worked through four continued wetlands hearings, voting to pursue a redesigned, wetland-avoiding ADA trail route at Cowry Nature Center and continuing three other hearings to September 16 due to late-submitted documents. The commission also voted to approve draft bylaw amendments to send toward town meeting, approved a $150 purchase for smoke/CO2 detectors at its Hollis Road property, and heard committee updates on storm water utility planning and mosquito-control drainage assistance.

what_happened.line: The Commission voted 5-0 to accept a redesigned ADA trail route at Cowry Nature Center that avoids direct wetland alteration.
Three other wetlands hearings -- a boat ramp, a driveway crossing, and an irrigation pond -- were continued to September 16 after documents arrived late.
The Commission voted 5-0 to approve draft bylaw amendments to move toward town meeting.
A storm water committee is drafting a warrant article for a storm water utility because the operating budget cannot fund the DPW's required catch-basin and culvert cleaning.
The Commission approved an amount as heard purchase for smoke and CO2 detectors at its Hollis Road property.

why_it_matters: The ADA trail redesign changes how a town-funded accessibility project reaches Cowry Nature Center and keeps it clear of wetland permitting delays.
The bylaw amendments the Commission approved will come before town meeting, where residents get a vote.
A storm water utility warrant article, if it advances, could mean a new fee tied to the town's stormwater permit obligations.
